extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters (court/city desk reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting criminal and civil court proceedings and related legal/community stories: courtroom Q&A, verdicts, appeals, legal opinions, and human-interest consequences. Emphasizes factual detail, legal tests, background, and narrative color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtroom Q&A transcript formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduce witness testimony and examination in a Q. / A. transcript style (questions and answers line-by-line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short labeled Q. and A. lines to present direct examination (e.g., 'Q. When you ran to the scene... A. On the south side.'), include exchanges verbatim where appropriate, and preserve the sequence of questioning to show how testimony unfolded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate heads for different parts of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize reports so that cross-examination and other parts of the day's proceedings are published under separate headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark transitions clearly (the text notes 'The report of the cross-examination and other details of the day's proceedings in the trial followed under separate heads') so readers can follow separate phases of a trial or hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include precise times and locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report exact times, streets, addresses, and locations where events occurred or where parties met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give clock times (e.g., '1:30 o'clock A. M.', 'direct examination ended at 11:02 A. M.'), street intersections and apartment names (e.g., '145th street and Seventh avenue', 'Belledaire apartments') to anchor the story in verifiable detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute quotes and identify speakers with roles
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoting, identify the speaker and their role (witness, attorney, judge, official) so readers understand authority and perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give full names and roles (e.g., 'Presiding Justice Gildersleeve', 'Attorney John Hart'), and attribute dialogue and paraphrase clearly (e.g., 'Becker said: "Don't mind anything. I'll fix it all right."').

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize legal rulings with test and citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the court's legal test or rule and, where relevant, cite precedent or case law used in the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the court's reasoning and any controlling rule (for example, the test of employer liability and citation 'Gervin vs. N. Y. Central R. R. Co., 166 N. Y. 289'), and note concurring opinions or authors of the opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide defendant's/subject's background and pattern of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Give relevant past history, aliases, prior convictions, and a pattern of behavior to contextualize the current charge or civil action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail prior incidents, aliases, prosecutions, and timelines (e.g., the Koch narrative listing aliases, past suits, imprisonments, and locations) to show whether present conduct is isolated or part of a pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report penalties, verdicts, and sentencing ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the announced verdict, the jury timeline, and the statutory or possible punishment range associated with the crime or civil judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State guilty/not guilty findings, jury retirement/return times, and the potential sentence (e.g., 'punishable by imprisonment... from one to ten years'), and note upcoming sentencing dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include human-interest detail and personal condition
rubrics_metrics.description: When stories have a personal or human-impact angle (injury, illness, family consequences), report the subject's condition, emotions, livelihood and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe injuries, medical prognosis, lifestyle changes and personal reactions (as in the Florence Lemoine piece: paralysis, hopes, occupation, family background) to convey consequence beyond legal formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include financial and transactional particulars in commercial/legal reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Report dollar amounts, creditor relationships, stock issues, dates, and the transactional mechanics behind corporate or claims stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give specific figures (e.g., '$2,600,000', '$1,000,000'), describe who holds paper or stock, explain alleged misstatements or accounting tricks, and outline remedies or receivership actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend narrative anecdote with procedural facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use narrative anecdotes and scene-setting to humanize procedural developments while preserving the essential procedural facts (orders, appointments, verdicts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine colorful detail (Baptiste Bardoli's trip, wine bottles, and behavior) with the legal outcomes (insanity jury verdict, conservator appointment, restoration orders) so the procedural record is readable and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey community voice and local color when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on immigrant societies, local committees, or community disputes, capture colloquial speech and cultural details to reflect community perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representative quotes, idiomatic phrasing and specific community names (e.g., the Kaminoka Strumolova anecdote) to show the reader how the community experienced or perceived the event — but balance color with clear factual reporting.
